intent: 10 canonical integrity laws, each triangulated in behavior, under pressure and prospective mechanism; vignette teaches coherence as intention/action alignment

assessment.intro: Think of the past 30 days. Answer based on what you actually did when you had a fair chance to choose. There is no penalty for skipping or saying a situation did not apply.

registers.meaning: How regularly the action occurred in eligible situations
How regularly action occurred in higher-cost opportunities
User's own anticipated outcome or protective reason, not proof of cause

assessment.results: OPTIONAL CORE10_SELF_REPORT_INDEX ONLY; never label as full 21-law CQ until a versioned and validated bridge to the canonical engine exists
assessment.privacy: No profile storage or journal inference without notice and permission; no sensitive raw entries in shareable link
assessment.onSkip: Unanswered and not-applicable remain NULL; never substitute 0
assessment.userAutonomy: Don't judge protective silence, sensible boundaries, disability, scarcity, exhaustion or coercion as automatically immoral

questions.prompt: When someone needed an honest answer, how often did you give it?
When honesty could upset someone, how often did you still tell the truth when safe?
When you held back, what were you afraid might happen?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The promise you didn't mean
vignette.story: A friend asks you to help this weekend. You already need rest, but you say yes to avoid disappointing them. By Saturday, you feel trapped and resentful.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You give an honest answer, even when it is uncomfortable. Both people can make a real choice.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You hide your limits to keep approval. The promise and your real intention drift apart.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the belief that an honest no will cost connection.
vignette.becomingAction: Give one respectful, truthful answer about what you can actually do.
vignette.contextBoundary: Privacy, danger and coercion are not failures to practice truth.

questions.prompt: When your choices affected someone, how often did you share what they needed to know?
When admitting a mistake felt embarrassing, how often did you tell them?
When you hid something important, what were you trying to protect?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The mistake no one saw
vignette.story: You spot an error in a shared project. Nobody else has noticed. If you say nothing, the team will make a decision using the wrong numbers.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You name the error and what it affects. Others can make informed choices and correct course.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You protect your image by hiding something relevant. People act on incomplete information.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the worry that admitting a mistake will make you less valuable.
vignette.becomingAction: Share one necessary fact clearly with the person affected.
vignette.contextBoundary: Transparency is not an obligation to share private or unsafe information.

questions.prompt: When someone disagreed with you, how often did you treat them with respect?
When your group judged someone, how often did you decide for yourself how to treat them?
When respect was difficult, what felt threatened?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The person everyone disagrees with
vignette.story: A group conversation turns against someone who sees things differently. You don't agree with them, but you notice people are talking as if they matter less.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You keep your judgment of an idea separate from your respect for a person.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You join in treating a person as less worthy because they differ from your group.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the need to belong that can overpower your own values.
vignette.becomingAction: Disagree with one idea without diminishing the person.
vignette.contextBoundary: Equal dignity doesn't require agreement or staying near someone unsafe.

questions.prompt: When someone was speaking, how often did you give them your attention?
When worry or distraction interrupted you, how often did you return to the moment?
When you drifted away, what drew your attention?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The conversation you missed
vignette.story: Someone close to you is telling you about a hard day. Your phone lights up. You keep checking it and miss what they actually needed.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You return your attention and understand more accurately what is being shared.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You leave the moment without noticing. Assumptions replace what was actually said.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice what pulls your attention away, without judging the distraction itself.
vignette.becomingAction: Put one distraction aside and listen long enough to reflect back what you heard.
vignette.contextBoundary: Pain, disability, nervous-system load and divided demands can limit attention; adjust expectations fairly.

questions.prompt: When someone struggled, how often did you take their feelings seriously?
When tired or annoyed, how often did you stay kind without ignoring your limits?
When you pulled away from someone's pain, what made it hard?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: Fixing when they needed listening
vignette.story: A colleague tells you they're overwhelmed. You immediately list solutions. Later you realize they needed to be heard before they could think about next steps.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You make space for the person's actual needs while keeping your own limits.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You try to stop your discomfort by fixing or dismissing the other person.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the urge to end discomfort quickly.
vignette.becomingAction: Ask once: 'Would listening or problem-solving help more?'
vignette.contextBoundary: Compassion does not require self-sacrifice, endless availability or ignoring boundaries.

questions.prompt: When something mattered but felt scary, how often did you take a reasonably safe step?
When speaking up might bring disapproval, how often did you speak when safe?
When you held back, what did you expect could happen?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The conversation you keep delaying
vignette.story: A workplace issue keeps coming back. You know a conversation could help, but you rehearse it for days because you're worried how it will land.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You take a proportionate, reasonably safe step aligned with what matters.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You avoid every possible step and let an important issue continue without review.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice whether rejection, conflict or uncertainty is driving the delay.
vignette.becomingAction: Choose one small, safe action toward the conversation.
vignette.contextBoundary: Declining to enter danger is sound judgment, not lack of courage.

questions.prompt: When you made a promise you could reasonably keep, how often did you follow through?
When you couldn't meet a commitment, how often did you tell the other person in time?
When a commitment slipped, what got in the way?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The yes that became too much
vignette.story: You agree to finish a task by Friday. New demands pile up, and by Wednesday you know you won't finish. You consider staying silent.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You keep workable promises, or speak up early so the other person can adapt.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You hide an impossible commitment and let others discover the cost too late.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the belief that disappointing someone makes you unworthy.
vignette.becomingAction: Renegotiate one commitment while there is still time.
vignette.contextBoundary: Forced obligations and unreasonable demands are not freely chosen duties.

questions.prompt: When a mistake affected someone, how often did you try to repair it?
When apologizing was uncomfortable, how often did you apologize directly when appropriate?
When you delayed repair, what stopped you?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The explanation before the apology
vignette.story: You forget something that mattered to a friend. When they mention it, you immediately describe how busy you've been. They still haven't heard you own the impact.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You name what you did, acknowledge the effect, and offer a proportionate repair.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You use a true explanation to avoid taking your share of responsibility.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice the fear that admitting a mistake makes you fundamentally bad.
vignette.becomingAction: Say what happened and ask what repair would be useful, when appropriate.
vignette.contextBoundary: Taking your share does not mean accepting blame for someone else's actions.

questions.prompt: When you'd had enough of something you wanted, how often did you stop?
When stressed, how often did you choose what you needed over an escape that left you worse off?
When you kept going past enough, what were you looking for?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: One more hour
vignette.story: You keep scrolling late at night, looking for a little relief after a hard day. An hour later, you're more tired and the relief hasn't lasted.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You recognize what you actually need and choose an action that supports it.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You keep reaching for more even when it is no longer helping.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice whether comfort, avoidance or habit is behind the next reach.
vignette.becomingAction: Pause at a familiar moment and choose rest, connection or another real need.
vignette.contextBoundary: Do not label health conditions or basic needs as lack of temperance.

questions.prompt: When upset, how often did you avoid unnecessary harm in what you said or did?
When setting a boundary, how often did you do it without trying to punish the other person?
When you wanted to hurt back, what felt threatened?

options: Something else, in my own words

vignette.title: The true but cutting reply
vignette.story: Someone upsets you. You have an accurate criticism ready, but you also know the way you could say it would be needlessly cruel.
vignette.alignedActionEffect: You state what is true and set a firm limit without adding unnecessary injury.
vignette.misalignedActionEffect: You use truth or silence as punishment and increase the damage.
vignette.releaseReflection: Notice what part of you wants the other person to feel the pain you felt.
vignette.becomingAction: Express one boundary without humiliation or retaliation.
vignette.contextBoundary: Protecting yourself or others from immediate harm is not the same as unnecessary aggression.
